confidence_why: Every description from San José 1610 through Bloomfield 1917, Schachter and Reid 2008 and Zuraw and Roca 2025 agrees that Tagalog words carry an unpredictable penult-or-ultima prominence with minimal pairs such as áso 'dog' and asó 'smoke', but whether that prominence is word stress (Bloomfield 1917, Hagberg 1993, Zuraw and Roca 2025) or a phonemic long penult plus default phrase-final accent (Schachter and Otanes 1972, Carrier 1979, Kaufman and Himmelmann 2024) is still argued.

catalog_quote: [Schachter & Reid] Vowel length in non-word-final syllables is phonemic, as the following examples illustrate: aso /?a:so/ 'dog', aso /?aso/ 'smoke' ... In word-final syllables of native words, vowel length is not phonemic: the general rule is that phrase-final syllables are long, non-phrase-final syllables short. ... Stress is closely tied to vowel length, with some analysts considering stress as primary, while others consider vowel length to be primary. Syllables with phonemically long vowels are always stressed. Syllables with vowels that are not phonemically long but are phonetically long as a result of their occurrence in phrase-final position are also stressed if there are no phonemically long vowels in the phrase-final word. sweep_summary: Tagalog (taga1270) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Schachter & Reid 2008. Of the 9 works with stress in the title: Hsieh 2016 (AFLA 23, read from the ANU OA volume) and Nagaya & Hwang 2018 (LangSci OA, read) are phrase-level prosody with no word-stress content (silent); Sabbagh 2014 (read in the lingbuzz preprint) states in passing, citing French 1988, that stress is contrastive and falls on the final or penultimate syllable (confirms). Three direct stress sources could not be read: Gonzalez 1981 'Tagalog accent revisited' (print only, LSP Monograph 2; high priority), French 1988 (the standard monograph every read paper cites; Glottolog's SIL URL is dead and SIL archive 22216 now points elsewhere; print only; high priority), French 1991 'Secondary stress in Tagalog' (JSTOR paywalled, doi 10.2307/3623086; medium). Brichoux 1972 is an 87-page MA thesis (California State College, LA), duplicated in Glottolog, not online (medium). Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Books 3) is open on sil.org but the PDF sits behind an automated-access block that automated download, direct download and headless/Xvfb Chrome all fail; its abstract (saved) treats Tagalog as a morphemic/floating-stress language (medium). Beyond the list, two open 2025 papers were read: Zuraw & Roca (Phonology, already held by the project) give corpus evidence that both penult- and ultima-prominent words bear phonological stress — the best first-hand statement found, refining and arguably superseding the hedged Schachter & Reid quote as the deciding source for 'lexical' — and Farinella & Jun (PLSA, downloaded now) restate unpredictable stress within a right-edge two-syllable window while staying agnostic on stress vs length. all lookups went through APIs (Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Glottolog.bib, Open Library, ANU/lingbuzz/Zenodo) and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: Words in Tagalog/Filipino can be either penult-prominent or ultima-prominent. Scholars have been divided on whether the language has stress, or only phonemic vowel length in penults and default phrase-final prominence. Using a corpus of Original Pilipino Music, we find that both prominent penults and prominent ultimas are set to longer notes and stronger beats, even in phrase-medial position. ... We conclude that songwriters' text-setting decisions reflect phonological stress in Filipino, and that both penult-prominent and ultima-prominent words bear stress. [p. 1] All this is evidence in favour of analysing Filipino as having stress [§10, p. 25]
new_statements.citation: Zuraw, Kie & Paolo Roca. 2025. Evidence for stress in Filipino text-setting. Phonology 42: e7, 1-30. doi:10.1017/S0952675725000041
new_statements.reading: Lexically contrastive word stress restricted to the last two syllables (penult or ultima; minimal pairs like ʔábot/ʔabót, búkas/bukás), with no root-anchored default; a first-hand corpus study concluding that the prominence is phonological stress rather than phonemic vowel length plus phrase-final accent. This supports the catalog's 'lexical' coding and is a stronger deciding statement than the hedged Schachter & Reid 2008 passage, whose own wording ('vowel length.. is phonemic', 'some analysts considering stress .') sits in the length camp. Caveat: the length analysis is still held by Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 / Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024, as both Zuraw & Roca and Farinella & Jun 2025 record.

new_statements.quote: The facts of Tagalog stress, as described in Ramos 1971, Schachter and Otanes 1972, Soberano 1980, French 1988 and Myers 1989, may be summarized as follows: Stress always falls on either the penultimate or final syllable, and for a given stem there is no way to predict from the phonology which of these two patterns will be observed. According to French 1988 (page 63), stress is realized phonetically as a relative peak of pitch and, on non-final syllables, phonetic vowel lengthening co-occurs with stress. [p. 317] ... Assuming that penultimate stress is unmarked in Tagalog, a single syllabic foot is constructed on the right edge of an unaccented word [p. 319] ... Tagalog stress is realized as both length and high pitch [p. 332]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the existing Zuraw & Roca 2025 statement (lexically contrastive stress, penult vs ultima); refines it with the penult-as-default analysis and the phonetic realization. Note the file opened is the archive.org 'opensource' upload of the 1993 UMI dissertation (Order 9328564), not the 2006 SIL e-Book revision (the SIL PDF is still an automated-access block-403); the data are second-hand from French 1988 and Soberano 1980 (Marinduque Tagalog).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically contrastive within a two-syllable right-edge window (penult or ultima); penultimate stress is the unmarked default, final stress is a lexical (floating) accent; stress is realized as pitch peak plus vowel length on non-final syllables. The stem's placement is preserved under most suffixation (p. 318), with two suffixes (-an nominal, -in) that shift stress (polarity effects).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Tagalog (only primary stress within the final two syllables is analysed).
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 32 (p. 317): Soberano 1980 instead treats all vowel length as underlying with stress assigned to long vowels; Hagberg rejects this following French 1988. Suffixes -an/-in shift stress rightward (pp. 322ff).

new_statements.quote: Almost without exception, closed syllables do not contain long vowels in native stems, either in derived or non-derived forms. Since all stem-final syllables are closed, they always contain a short vowel. Penultimate syllables, however, may be open or closed. For those stems whose penultimate syllable is open, the length of the penultimate vowel is not predictable from any other phonological properties of the stem. This is clear from the following minimal pairs. [p. 119; 168a ?asoh 'dog' / e. ?a:soh 'smoke' etc.] ... Most native stems are disyllabic, but some are trisyllabic or longer. Still, in these longer stems, only the penultimate syllable and no syllable farther to the left can contain a long vowel. Again, the length of the penultimate vowel is an idiosyncratic property of the stem. [p. 120]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees on a lexically unpredictable two-way contrast confined to the last two syllables, but frames it as phonemic penultimate vowel length rather than stress, i.e. the 'length camp' that the existing statement records as a caveat (Himmelmann & Kaufman); it does not argue against a stress analysis explicitly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress section: the prominence contrast is analysed as underlying vowel LENGTH, contrastive only on an open penultimate syllable and idiosyncratic per stem (long penult = penult-prominent, short penult = final-prominent); no syllable left of the penult can be long; length is shifted or removed by affixation rules. 'Stressed'/'unstressed' vowels are used informally in the flapping and preglide-deletion sections (sec. IE-IF, pp. 148-160) without definition.
new_statements.exceptions: Closed syllables never long ('almost without exception'); suffixation with -in/-an lengthens the stem-final vowel and shortens the underlying penult (pp. 120-125); some stems optionally lose penultimate length.

new_statements.quote: Acento, en su concepto gramatical, es la mayor intensidad con que se hiere determinada sílaba, al pronunciar una palabra. En tagalo, el acento es muy indispensable para distinguir una palabra de otra, porque en la mayoría de los casos, el acento es el único que determina la diversidad de significado de los vocablos que tienen igual estructura. Las palabras por razón del acento, pueden ser agudas, llanas, esdrújulas y sobreesdrújulas. [p. 10] Son palabras agudas, cuando el acento carga en la última sílaba. Ejemplo:— Anó, (qué), matá, (ojo), maliksí (ágil), etc. Son palabras llanas, cuando el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba. Ejemplo:— Sákit (pena,) búhay (vida), táo (persona), etc. Son palabras esdrújulas, cuando el acento carga en la antepenúltima sílaba. Ejemplo: Dálitá, (sufrimiento) líbingan, (sepultura), úliran (modelo) etc. [p. 11]
new_statements.translation: Accent, in its grammatical sense, is the greater intensity with which a given syllable is struck when a word is pronounced. In Tagalog the accent is absolutely indispensable for distinguishing one word from another, because in most cases the accent is the only thing that determines the difference in meaning between words of identical structure. By their accent, words can be oxytone, paroxytone, proparoxytone and pre-proparoxytone. [p. 10] Words are oxytone when the accent falls on the last syllable, e.g. anó 'what', matá 'eye', maliksí 'agile'. Words are paroxytone when the accent falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. sákit 'pain', búhay 'life', táo 'person'. Words are proparoxytone when the accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. dálitá 'suffering', líbingan 'grave', úliran 'model'. [p. 11]
new_statements.citation: Iganacio, Rosendo (1921). Nueva gramatica Hispano-Tagala. Imp. P. Sayo balo ni Soriano.

new_statements.relation_note: Same lexical type and the same penult/ultima contrast with minimal pairs, but it also places accent on the antepenult and earlier syllables in derived words, beyond the two-syllable window of the existing Zuraw & Roca statement (these look like secondary stresses on prefixes and reduplicants rather than a contradiction of the primary-stress window).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (defined as intensity) is contrastive and unpredictable: it distinguishes otherwise identical words (p. 235 list 'palabras de doble acepción': aso 'dog' / asó 'smoke', balat / balát, bilog / bilóg..); it may fall on the ultima or penult, and in longer (derived) words on the antepenult or the fourth/fifth syllable from the end (mánunulat 'writer'). Grave and circumflex marks on final vowels indicate a final glottal ('gutural') vowel, short/paused vs short, not a different accent position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such, but the esdrújula and sobreesdrújula examples (dálitá, líbingan, úliran, mánunulat, mámamahayag) mark prominence on prefix/reduplicant syllables of derived words, i.e. what later work calls secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with grave/circumflex (final glottal) lose that sound when joined to ligatures (p. 11); p. 234 distinguishes 'orthographic' accent (written, final: kulóg, balát) from 'prosodic' accent (unwritten, penultimate: tubig, sulat, aso).

new_statements.quote: The acute accent may fall upon any syllable, but in Tagalog is generally to be found upon the last (ultima) or the next to the last syllable (penultima). ... In many cases the suffixing of 'han' or 'hin' draws the accent one syllable farther toward the end of the word. This also applies to 'an' or 'in.' ... It may be taken as a rule that words unmarked with an accent, if ending with a consonant, take the accent upon the ultima, words ending with n and s being excepted. Words ending with an unaccented vowel or 'n' or 's' generally take the accent upon the penultima. This is also the rule in Spanish. [p. 18] Practice is the essential requirement to become familiar with the accent, which is most important in Tagalog, as many words are only distinguished by the accent, although differing totally in meaning. Example: Asó, 'smoke;' áso, 'dog;' gátas, 'milk;' gatás, 'path, trail;' [p. 19]
new_statements.citation: MacKinlay, William Egbert Wheeler (1905). A handbook and grammar of the Tagalog language. Washington: Govt. Print. Off. 264 pp.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent is generally on the ultima or penult and is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs asó/áso, gátas/gatás, sumílang/sumilang, bumása/bumasá); the 'rule' for unmarked words (consonant-final = ultima, vowel/n/s-final = penult) is the Spanish orthographic convention for writing accents, not a phonological placement rule. Suffixes -han/-hin/-an/-in draw the accent one syllable rightward.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; p. 18 notes the acute is written on the penultima or antepenultima of consonant-final words.
new_statements.exceptions: Grave and circumflex marks denote a final short/abrupt vowel (glottal stop), not a different stress; the circumflex marks a final glottal vowel that carries the stress. Later sections note accent shifts under affixation, plural by accent shift (p. 19604 region of the text).

new_statements.quote: Dos son los acentos más usados en este idioma: el uno es de pronunciación aguda, y el otro de suave. ... Póngase especial cuidado en la pronunciación, á fin de evitar equivocaciones que dan por resultado decir una cosa por otra, si bien con las mismas palabras, pero de diversa significación. [p. 19] Los acentos principales son cuatro, á saber: Penúltima grave producta, y se señala en el Diccionario con esta nota, pp., v. g.: Aso.—Penúltima grave pausal, pp.ᵃ Vicá.—Penúltima correpta grave, pc. Asó.—Penúltima correpta gutural, pc.ᵃ Duc-há. El vocablo de acento penúltima correpta se pronuncia como hiriendo á la última sílaba, v. g.: Tapát, pc. En frente. [p. 430] ... Para saber qué raices piden el acento gutural, ó penúltima producta pausal, no hay regla fija. [p. 432]
new_statements.translation: There are two accents most used in this language: one of sharp (final) pronunciation and one of soft. ... Take special care in pronunciation, to avoid mistakes which result in saying one thing for another, with the same words but different meaning. [p. 19] The principal accents are four: long grave penult, marked in the dictionary pp., e.g. aso 'dog'; long paused penult, pp.ᵃ, vicá; short grave penult, pc., asó 'smoke'; short guttural penult, pc.ᵃ, duc-há. A word with short-penult accent is pronounced as if striking the last syllable, e.g. tapát 'in front'. [p. 430] ... To know which roots take the guttural accent or the long paused penult, there is no fixed rule. [p. 432]

new_statements.relation_note: Same two-way lexical contrast penult vs ultima (aso/asó, tapát vs sulat) as the catalog and the Zuraw & Roca statement; refines with the traditional four-way pp/pc x glottal classification, the 'no fixed rule' statement, and morphological tendencies.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two basic accents: long penult (pp, banayar = penult prominence, 'as we pronounce malo, bueno') vs short penult (pc, sarlác = prominence on the final syllable, 'as our preterites amó, corrió'), each subdivided by presence of a final glottal ('pausal'/'gutural'); the root's accent is a lexical property with no fixed rule, though CVC-CVC reduplicated roots and trisyllables with identical last two syllables regularly take pc (pp. 432-433), and roots denoting speed take pc while roots denoting slowness take pp; affixation frequently changes the root accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Regla primera-tercera (p. 432-433): reduplicated consonant-final roots are pc; reduplicated disyllabic compounds (biling-biling, ala-ala) are pp; monosyllabic particles bear no accent (p. 431); many derivational categories change or preserve the root accent (nombres de lugar, instrumento etc., pp. 285ff).

new_statements.quote: Baste aquí el decir que son dos los acentos; el uno es largo, y se denota en el Vocabulario con esta cifra pc, á quien llama el tagalog Sarlác. El otro es breve, y se denota con esta pp, llaman banáyar. A los cuales por la brevedad y facilidad mayor, se acentuarán en este arte, como en el latín y en el castellano se acentúa; al largo en la última y al breve en la penúltima, ó antepenúltima. Vg.: acó, que largo significa yo y se denota así pc, se acentuará de este modo, hiriendo á la última sílaba. Acó, y el mismo, que breve significa fiar, y se apunta así pp se acentuará hiriendo en la sílaba primera áco. ... Otros dos acentos hay en este idioma, á quienes llaman cortadillos
new_statements.translation: Let it suffice here to say that there are two accents: one is long, marked in the Vocabulary with the sign pc, which the Tagalog calls sarlác; the other is short, marked pp, which they call banáyar. For brevity and greater ease they will be accented in this Arte as in Latin and Spanish: the long on the last syllable and the short on the penultimate or antepenultimate. E.g. acó, which with the long accent means 'I' and is marked pc, will be accented by striking the last syllable, acó; and the same word, which with the short accent means 'to trust/lend' and is marked pp, will be accented by striking the first syllable, áco. ... There are two further accents in this language, which they call cortadillos (the glottal-final types).

The front-matter Advertencia primera defines the notation: 'Pen. prod. quiere decir penultima producta, q̃ es decir, que la syllaba que antecede à la vltima sea larga, y espaciosa en aquella palabra, cuyo accento se declara. Morphological accent shifts are noted throughout the verb chapters (e.g. cap. 5 reg. 3, p. 290: in nagbabanalbanalan the accent stops on the first syllable of the root and again on the penult).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence is contrastive (the author declines to decide whether the contrast is stress or vowel length) and falls on one of the last two syllables: either a long stressed penult or a short penult with a stressed ultima. A long/stressed penult must be open in native words; antepenultimate stress/length occurs only in a few loans. Under the most common suffixation, stress and length shift one syllable to the right (p. 130: 'if the bare stem has final stress, stress falls on the suffix; if the bare stem has penultimate stress and length, the penult of the suffixed form has stress and length'; p. 165: hé:ro 'brand', heru:-han 'to brand'; sermón, sermun-án).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'In derived words, there may be length and secondary stress on the antepenult or earlier syllables' (fn. 9); in disyllabic reduplication the reduplicant bears secondary stress on its long penult, otherwise on its ultima (p. 144); long vowels with no marked stress are secondary-stressed (p. 13). Some affixes cause unpredictable stress/length shifts (table 18, p. 34).
new_statements.exceptions: A few loans with antepenultimate stress and length; loans with long stressed closed penults behave differently under suffixation; certain nasal-substituting affixes induce unpredictable stress/length shifts.

The main stress of a Tagalog stem is either ultimate or penultimate. [p. 64] ... Departing from Schachter and Otanes, I claim that stress, not vowel length, is contrastive. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (word-level) stress is lexically contrastive and falls on either the ultima or the penult of the stem (minimal pairs búkas/bukás, púnoʔ/punóʔ; also word-class pairs búhay 'life' vs buháy 'alive'); vowel length is treated as the phonetic consequence of stress on a non-final syllable, explicitly rejecting the Schachter & Otanes / Soberano / Carrier length analysis. In verbs the stem's stress position (ultima vs penult) is preserved across all inflectional and focus paradigms: word-level stress is copied onto the corresponding syllable of stem(+suffix) after the last resyllabification, so suffixation shifts it rightward to stay penultimate/ultimate (rules 129-130, p. 66; (146a), p. 72).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Treated at length with Prince (1983) grid theory (secs. 3.2-3.7). Prefix and stem(+suffix) are separate stress domains. Rules (145)-(146), pp. 71-72: the first syllable of a polysyllabic prefix gets foot-level (secondary) stress (End Rule 1), except that ʔi- prefixes stress their second syllable (ER2) and a heavy CVC prefix syllable attracts the secondary stress (HS); an inflected (reduplicated/infixed) prefix copies the stress position of its basic form unless a clash results (CX); a syllable resulting from reduplication in the stem gets secondary stress (RSS) and a reduplicated prefix syllable gets word-level prominence (RSP). Monosyllabic prefixes get no secondary stress; plural-adjective reduplication adds none (p. 83). ka- -an nouns (160), pp. 82-83: secondary stress on the antepenult when the stem is CVCVC, otherwise by right-to-left alternating Perfect Grid; diminutive adjectives (170), p. 87. Secondary stress alone distinguishes homophones such as magsàsákah 'farmer' vs magsasákah 'will farm', ka-ʔìbig-án 'mutual consent' vs ka-ʔibig-án 'preference' (sec. 3.6, pp. 87-89). Perfect-grid alternation otherwise has little application: Tagalog tends to one clear prominence per constituent, with long 'unbounded' feet (p. 91).
new_statements.exceptions: Derived ka- -an nouns do not keep the stem's stress: a penult-stressed disyllabic stem gives an ultima-stressed noun (báyad -> kabayarán) and an ultima-stressed one a penult-stressed noun (tiyák -> katiyákan), a predictable but non-'autosegmental' shift (p. 82); táwaʔ 'laugh' shifts to ultimate stress under nakaka-/ka- (fn. 10, p. 84); accepted variants that break the rules, e.g. kapayapàʔán, magsasakáh 'farmer', matalitalínoh (223), p. 117; sàkáyan/bìgáyan-type derived stems keep their own penultimate stress (fn. 7, p. 65); baligtad (speech-disguise) data give only inconclusive support for stress as an autosegment (sec. 4.4, pp. 107-109).

readall_conflicts: All six opened works agree that Tagalog prominence is lexically distinctive and confined to a penult-vs-ultima contrast (Totanes 1865 acó/áco; Coria 1872 aso/asó, tapát; MacKinlay 1905 asó/áso, gátas/gatás; Ignacio 1921 aso/asó, balat/balát; Hagberg 1993 ?asoh/?a:soh; Carrier 1979 ?asoh/?a:soh). The disagreements are about type and window. Type: Carrier 1979 analyses the contrast as underlying penultimate vowel LENGTH (pp. 118-120), the length camp, whereas Hagberg 1993 (following French 1988, and noting Soberano 1980's length analysis in fn. 32) treats it as stress realized as pitch peak plus length on non-final syllables (pp. 317, 332); the missionary grammars use 'acento' with quantity terms (largo/breve, producta/correpta). Window: Ignacio 1921 (p. 11) places accent on the antepenult and fourth/fifth syllable in derived words (dálitá, líbingan, mánunulat), and Totanes allows the 'short' accent on the antepenult, going beyond the two-syllable window; these are prefix/reduplicant prominences (secondary stress) rather than a different primary-stress system. sources.quote: Almost without exception, closed syllables do not contain long vowels in native stems, either in derived or non-derived forms. Since all stem-final syllables are closed, they always contain a short vowel. Penultimate syllables, however, may be open or closed. For those stems whose penultimate syllable is open, the length of the penultimate vowel is not predictable from any other phonological properties of the stem. This is clear from the following minimal pairs. [p. 119; 168a ?asoh 'dog' / e. ?a:soh 'smoke' etc.] ... Most native stems are disyllabic, but some are trisyllabic or longer. Still, in these longer stems, only the penultimate syllable and no syllable farther to the left can contain a long vowel. Again, the length of the penultimate vowel is an idiosyncratic property of the stem. [p. 120]

sources.quote: Acento, en su concepto gramatical, es la mayor intensidad con que se hiere determinada sílaba, al pronunciar una palabra. En tagalo, el acento es muy indispensable para distinguir una palabra de otra, porque en la mayoría de los casos, el acento es el único que determina la diversidad de significado de los vocablos que tienen igual estructura. Las palabras por razón del acento, pueden ser agudas, llanas, esdrújulas y sobreesdrújulas. [p. 10] Son palabras agudas, cuando el acento carga en la última sílaba. Ejemplo:— Anó, (qué), matá, (ojo), maliksí (ágil), etc. Son palabras llanas, cuando el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba. Ejemplo:— Sákit (pena,) búhay (vida), táo (persona), etc. Son palabras esdrújulas, cuando el acento carga en la antepenúltima sílaba. Ejemplo: Dálitá, (sufrimiento) líbingan, (sepultura), úliran (modelo) etc. [p. 11]

sources.quote: The acute accent may fall upon any syllable, but in Tagalog is generally to be found upon the last (ultima) or the next to the last syllable (penultima). ... In many cases the suffixing of 'han' or 'hin' draws the accent one syllable farther toward the end of the word. This also applies to 'an' or 'in.' ... It may be taken as a rule that words unmarked with an accent, if ending with a consonant, take the accent upon the ultima, words ending with n and s being excepted. Words ending with an unaccented vowel or 'n' or 's' generally take the accent upon the penultima. This is also the rule in Spanish. [p. 18] Practice is the essential requirement to become familiar with the accent, which is most important in Tagalog, as many words are only distinguished by the accent, although differing totally in meaning. Example: Asó, 'smoke;' áso, 'dog;' gátas, 'milk;' gatás, 'path, trail;' [p. 19]

sources.quote: Stress, which is contrastive in Tagalog, generally falls either on the final or the penultimate syllable of a word regardless of the number of syllables (French 1988:63-65). Assuming that stress is associated with the prosodic category Foot, the position of stress in words can be taken to suggest that feet are parsed from right-to-left in Tagalog. Right-to-left parsing of feet will leave any un-footed syllables—e.g., in odd syllable words—to be (stray) adjoined at the prosodic word level. Hence, three syllable words such as siyásat ('investigation') and talagá ('surely') have the schematic prosodic structure shown in (71).

sources.quote: Tagalog has a word level relative prominence distinction which has been analyzed as either a vowel length contrast or stress. On the latter analysis, Tagalog roots have unpredictable stress within a two syllable window at the right edge of words (Bloomfield 1917; French 1988). This gives rise to minimal pairs such as /"aso/ (dog) and /as"o/ (smoke). The other approach claims that Tagalog has a vowel length contrast on penultimate syllables in roots (Schachter & Otanes 1972; Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024; Kaufman To appear). ... The purpose of this paper is not to make claims about the word level prosodic system of Tagalog, but about intonation.
sources.note: Intonation study (AP/iP/IP edge tones). Restates the placement fact — unpredictable prominence on penult or ultima, minimal pairs — and the two analyses, stays agnostic on stress vs length; finds AP-initial tones only optionally align to the prominent syllable (Figs 7-8, words with penult and with final 'stress'), i.e. word-level prominence is visible to the intonation system phrase-medially.
